newsitem.title: UK: BA expects to run 95 pct of flights Monday.
newsitem.headline: BA expects to run 95 pct of flights Monday.

text.p: British Airways Plc said on Friday it anticipated 95 percent of its flights worldwide would operate from Monday as staff continued to trickle back to work after last week's cabin crew strike.

A BA spokesman said about 150 flight attendants a day were returning from sick leave since the strike ended last Friday, but 1,200 were still off sick -- twice the number normally expected for this time of year.
Services out of London Gatwick are already back to normal. And the airline said it planned to operate all but a handful of flights from London Heathrow.
Nearly 2,000 cabin crew registered for sick leave last week. This meant only 313 staff were actually registered as being on strike.

The airline and the BASSA cabin crew union -- representing nearly 9,000 members -- have agreed to reopen talks in the dispute over pay, after BASSA offered to make new proposals on how to find the 42 million pounds of savings sought by management from a new pay structure.
However, BA said BASSA, part of the Transport and General Workers Union (T&G), had not yet submitted its proposals on making the savings.
A union spokeswoman confirmed the union was still drafting them and the documents could be sent to BA's management "at some point next week."
T&G representative Andrew Murray said on Wednesday that once BA received its proposals, negotiations would begin. Talks are expected to take two to three weeks.
BA said on Tuesday the strike had already cost the company "tens of millions of pounds" as well as lost bookings for the future and urged BASSA to adopt a "constructive approach."
The 3,000 members of the breakaway union, Cabin Crew 89 which represents about 25 percent of BA's cabin staff, have already accepted the company's new pay package.
A separate dispute between BA and its ground staff over the sale of its in-house catering plant at Heathrow was virtually settled, both BA and union officials said.
